answer.evidence: The stair run is drawn as repeated treads. Each tread is a 5-6 row band (rows 21-25, 29-34, 38-43) that ends in a 1-row light front-edge line (rows 26, 35, 44) followed by 2 rows of dark shadow (rows 27-28, 36-37, 45-47). This is evidence (a) for a top surface. The gold landing at rows 10-12 has its own edge line at row 12 and shadow at rows 13-14. The risers are thin, only 2-3 rows of shadow. The dark flanking walls act as the vertical frame. The top strip at rows 0-2 is a front-facing cornice and is not counted as a top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair-up wall niche with a grey stone arch, a red runner and a light stone frame. It reads at about 4 shading steps per material, against roughly 5-6 in the references. Measured visible tones per tile are 11, below the timber reference (17) and the stone reference (13) but not far from the stone one. Near-flat coverage is 8%, while both references are at 0%. This indicates a few flat patches, probably in the red runner and the dark interior. Dark edge pixels are only 13% neutral, matching the references, so the outlines lean toward a tint rather than black. The stone arch has some per-block shading but less grain than the references' stones and plaster speckle. Overall it is close to the reference but a little thinner and flatter, and with some flat areas it falls just short of the Beodeul bar.

answer.evidence: The main body is a staircase with a red carpet, drawn as repeated tread bands. Each band is 5-6 stone rows (21-25, 29-34, 38-43) that end in a light front-edge line (rows 26, 35, 44) followed by 2-3 dark shadow rows (27-28, 36-37, 45-47). That is evidence (a), repeated for each step. The step risers and flanking walls are vertical faces of 3 or more rows. No isometric side face is drawn. The top lintel and arch area is mostly a front-facing gold band with dark shadow below, but the stair treads carry the top-surface evidence.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone arch with a red runner stair. Its arch stones and the red carpet each show about 4 tones, a little under the references' 5-6 per material. Visible tones per tile are 11, against 13 for the stone reference and 17 for the timber reference, so slightly lower but close to the stone wall. Only 8% of it is near-flat, with no large single-colour areas. Only 13% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, the same as the timber reference, so the outlines lean toward the neighbouring material (dark stone grey, dark red-brown) and don't read as a black sticker line. The stones and steps have some per-block shading, though less grain than the reference stone wall. A careful artist could accept it next to the stone reference without it looking clearly flatter, so it passes narrowly.

answer.evidence: The staircase repeats a tread band, then a 1-row light front-edge line (rows 18, 26, 35, 44), then 2-3 rows of dark shadow for the riser (rows 19-20, 27-28, 36-37, 45-47). The treads are 5-7 rows tall and the carpet runs across them. The gold landing at rows 10-12 is also a horizontal band with a front edge and shadow below. The risers are thin, but they are present. The overall read is stairs seen from above at about 45 degrees rather than a flat elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone arch with a red-carpeted stair. Its dark edge pixels are only 13% neutral, the same as the timber reference (13%) and close to the stone one (12%), so the outline is tinted dark material tone, not a sticker line. The arch blocks and carpet bands show about 4 lightness steps per material, against about 6 on the references. It has 11 visible tones per tile against 17 (timber) and 13 (stone), so it is below both. Near-flat coverage is 8% against 0% on both references, so some blocks of the carpet and the stair risers are flat fills. Total distinct colours are 15 against 68 and 33, meaning less per-stone shading and grain. It is clean and readable but a little thinner than the references, so I fail it on the borderline rule.
